  misses. Best case local, worst case a parallel fan-out.
- **Unsatisfied claim polls fan out.** Locality-optimized search only stops at
  the local partition when the query's `LIMIT` is already satisfied there. An
  idle or partially-filled poll — the common case for these low-volume queues —

  latency is roughly the slowest region's RTT rather than the sum, but it means
  the win is concentrated on **busy** polls and on the post-ack DELETE, not on

  (see the footgun above).
- **Unique constraints on an RBR table cost a cross-region uniqueness check per

266 docs/auth.md
1:# entire auth
7:## The shape of it
19:## Terminology
23:| **account** (a **user** or a **service account**) | a SpiceDB principal a customer creates and manages — a person, or a machine identity they create ("a user that isn't a person"); one subject type covers both | an **automation identity** or an **internal workload** — neither is an account |
25:| **account access token** (aka a **login token** for a user, an **SA token** for a service account) | gives access to your *account*: presented directly to entire-core and to every resource server, authorized live against SpiceDB at whichever one receives it | a pre-scoped resource credential — it carries identity only, not a baked-in permission |
45:## 1. Principals
49:### 1.1 Account
51:A SpiceDB principal — a single `account` subject type spanning two forms, a human and a service account. A customer creates both deliberately, names them, and they outlive any particular use. (How accounts are authorized: [section 3.1](#31-accounts).)
53:#### 1.1.1 Human user
59:#### 1.1.2 Service account
65:### 1.2 Automation identity
70:- **Display:** the token also carries a `handle` claim of `<class>/<job>` (e.g. `runner/trail-slop`, `ci/entiredb`). It is attribution only: entiredb copies it to the `entire.handle` span attribute, and no authorization decision reads it.
74:### 1.3 Internal workload
76:entire's own first-party services, such as entire-core, entiredb, and mirror-worker.
80:entiredb's data-plane nodes are internal workloads too, peering node-to-node (replication, repair). (How workloads are authorized: [section 3.3](#33-internal-workloads).)
82:### 1.4 Break-glass operator
84:A human recovering a cluster when entire-core (and therefore SpiceDB) is unreachable.
86:- **Identifier:** none real — `sub` is the zero ULID, `iss="entiredb"`. Self-signed by the cluster's local key, never by entire-core. (How it authorizes, offline: [section 3.4](#34-break-glass).)
90:## 2. Authentication
94:### 2.1 Humans and service accounts
100:entire-core's own `/api/v1` is one of those resource servers: it accepts the account access token minted by any core in `JURISDICTION_AUTH_HOSTS`, verified against that core's JWKS with `aud == iss`, no exchange ([ADR 20260902](adrs/20260902-sibling-login-jwt-on-core-api.md)).
102:### 2.2 Automation identities
111:- **Plugin JWT** (`pluginToken`): a JWT a cataloged plugin signs for one of its installations. The token's `plugin_id` claim names the plugin. Core verifies the token with that plugin's JWKS or registered keys and requires the plugin's issuer.
116:### 2.3 Internal workloads
120:### 2.4 Break-glass operator
126:## 3. Authorization
128:Accounts and automation identities resolve live against SpiceDB; internal workloads do not.
130:### 3.1 Accounts
132:Account authorization lives in SpiceDB. Humans and service accounts use the same subject type. Resource grants determine their access to customer resources.
136:An account presents the **account access token** everywhere, and the resource server resolves authorization **live against SpiceDB on each request**: the token says only *who you are*; what you may do is answered freshly, at the resource.
138:A workload may also act **on behalf of** an account (OBO) — carrying the account's access token with an `act` claim naming itself. Authorization is unchanged: the resource server resolves the account's identity live, exactly as above; the `act` claim only records the acting workload, for audit. (Who may act for whom is decided when the token is issued, not at the resource server.) entire-mcp is the first such workload: it exchanges the connector token a user gave it for this shape ([ADR 20260924](adrs/20260924-mcp-on-behalf-of-account-access-token.md)). One surface reads `act`: entire-core's console and admin gates refuse a delegated token whose actor this core authenticated (`act.iss` equals the token's `iss`), because a workload acting for an account is not the account's own console session. A federated SA session also carries `act`, naming the external issuer; it is the SA's own session and passes.
140:### 3.2 Automation identities
142:Automation identities authorize the same way accounts do — live against SpiceDB on every request, from grants on the resources they act on. They occupy the same grant relations an account does (`repo#reader`, `repo#writer`), so a job's authority is shaped by which grant it holds, not by a parallel set of automation-only permissions. Eight rules are specific to them:
144:- **A matching binding is required to issue the credential.** The registered provider alone isn't the trust anchor: the exchange also requires a binding tying that provider to this specific automation, whose attribute filter the assertion's claims must satisfy. No binding, no credential — fail closed.
145:- **No ambient authority.** No permission arm admits an automation subject by wildcard, so an automation identity holds exactly the grants written for it. The guarantee is structural: SpiceDB wildcards are scoped to a subject type.
150:- **A trail's body is the one grant outside this shape.** An automation identity is expected to hold at most one live `trail#editor` grant at a time, conferring `write_body` on the one trail its run produced output for — a caller-side convention, not a SpiceDB-enforced constraint. Unlike the repo grants above, this is issued one-shot by an internal grant endpoint at run start rather than reconciled from configuration, and the schema makes its expiry mandatory rather than optional — it is a run-scoped credential, not a standing one.
153:When a service-account principal pushes to a GitHub mirror, entiredb cannot use
158:cache hits; entiredb uses it only for the synchronous upstream push and then
166:For a mirror, entiredb requests a single-repository `contents:write` token under
170:the run-to-code-repo and code-repo-to-storage-repo bindings, and entiredb admits
175:inside entiredb limits credential exposure without removing the publisher's
179:capability) before the entiredb git plane (which starts requesting it), and roll
185:### 3.3 Internal workloads
187:Internal workloads follow the mainstream zero-trust shape ([section 4](#4-references-and-prior-art)): **the certificate proves identity; each resource server decides what that identity may do from its own local inbound allowlist.** Authority is something the *resource server* declares about its callers, not something the caller carries — no bearer token, no SpiceDB lookup. A service knows only the callers it serves.
189:The permissions are static and **class-scoped**. Each service may enforce them differently — all-or-nothing access, per-route access, and so on. entiredb's git mount, for example, admits entiredb peer-fetch and peregrine on **read-any-repo** (cluster-wide pull) and mirror-worker on **write-mirror** (pull plus push to mirror-class repos).
193:### 3.4 Break-glass
195:Break-glass authorizes *without* SpiceDB and *without* a remote issuer — the credential itself carries the authority, trusted on its signature. Since all account authz is a live SpiceDB lookup, it is the only human path that works when SpiceDB or entire-core is down. It stays **admin-only** (recovery runs through admin operations, not raw git) and is audited distinctly.
197:### 3.5 GitHub credential redemption
201:A subject admitted only through push scope requires the authenticated entiredb workload on the internal mTLS listener.
212:## 4. References and prior art
232:- **Google Zanzibar** — the central store is for *online user → object* permissions; service-identity authz is a separate plane. (SpiceDB is a Zanzibar implementation.) <https://research.google/pubs/zanzibar-googles-consistent-global-authorization-system/>
